articles.title: Deadly fire breaks out at Canada military base
articles.summary: Defence Minister David McGuinty says there are casualties in what the prime minister called a "serious incident".
articles.body:
A large fire near a Canadian military base in Alberta has killed and injured some people, the defence minister said, without confirming the number of casualties.

The Canadian Armed Forces were working with local authorities to manage the fire and were looking into what caused it, David McGuinty said, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate".

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said on X that a "serious incident creating a major fire" had occurred, adding his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected".

Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where the fire broke out, is one of the country's busiest military training bases.

The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation describes it as "the principal base for live fire training exercises". About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a regular day, according to the CBC.

Saturday's blaze "spread rapidly due to high winds" and had torn through the fences of the base, the Municipal District of Wainwright said.

McGuinty told reporters he "cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory".

Alberta's premier Danielle Smith says the "significant and tragic fire" is "affecting many of [the province's] brave military personnel". Provincial authorities are in touch with the central government in managing and investigating the situation, she added.

It is unclear when the fire broke out, but the district first posted about the incident at about 17:30 local time (23:30 GMT).

Local authorities have urged residents to avoid the area and give all emergency vehicles right of way.

Neighbouring provinces have offered their support.

Saskatchewan premier Scott Moe says he has deployed resources to Alberta and is "ready to provide more if required", while British Columbia premier David Eby says his government has "reached out to Alberta to offer all possible assistance".

articles.title: 5,50,000 on streets: How cost-of-living anger is sweeping Europe
articles.summary: Protests over the rising cost of living swept France, Belgium, Italy and Portugal on Saturday, as thousands of people took to the streets over economic
articles.body: Protests over the rising cost of living swept France, Belgium, Italy and Portugal on Saturday, as thousands of people took to the streets over economic pressures, housing affordability and education costs.Demonstrations in France drew the largest crowds, while unrest in other countries reflected growing discontent over wages, university fees and access to housing.According to Al Jazeera, the protests were driven by country-specific grievances, although demonstrators shared concerns about the cost of living and public services.While housing and low wages dominated protests in Portugal, student concerns over education costs fuelled demonstrations in Belgium. In France, protests extended beyond living costs to school conditions and public spending, while demonstrations in Italy also included opposition to wars.France witnessed one of its most turbulent days of protests in decades on Saturday, with more than 550,000 people taking part in demonstrations across the country, according to Al Jazeera.The protests began last month with high school students highlighting teacher shortages, deteriorating school facilities and overcrowded classrooms before expanding into a broader movement against inequality, rising prices and declining public services.President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm ahead of the demonstrations, defending the right to protest while warning against violence.“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself,” he said, adding that the right required respect for people and property.In Portugal, tens of thousands of people marched through Lisbon against rising living costs, low wages and a worsening housing crisis. Protesters, mobilised by the country's main trade union confederation, demanded higher wages and pensions and action on housing and fuel costs.Portuguese Parliamentary affairs minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said the government would not give in to pressure from street demonstrations, stating that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street”.Protesters, meanwhile, accused political leaders of being “out of touch” with the difficulties faced by ordinary households.In Belgium, several hundred mostly young protesters clashed with police in Brussels on Saturday, opposing rising education costs and reforms they fear could make higher education less accessible. Police deployed tear gas and water cannon after some demonstrators overturned a car, while protests also took place in the eastern city of Liège.Belgian interior minister Bernard Quintin condemned the violence, saying, “What is unfolding in Brussels is no longer mere protest,” and warned that “all necessary means will be used to restore order in the face of the rioters”.In Italy, demonstrations over the cost of living in Milan and Bologna turned violent on Saturday, with protesters throwing stones at police and officers deploying tear gas and water cannon to disperse crowds.Italian media reported injuries and arrests, while police in Bologna arrested seven people after clashes.Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence while defending peaceful demonstrations. “Demonstrating is a right. Turning our cities into battlegrounds is not,” she said in a post on X.She also urged opposition parties to condemn the violence and called for protests to remain peaceful.Alberto Alemanno, professor of EU law and policy at HEC Paris, told Al Jazeera that the protests could spread to other European countries, including Greece, Germany and Austria.He said the demonstrations were not part of a single coordinated movement but reflected shared grievances over rising living costs, underfunded education and uncertainty over employment prospects.Alemanno said the protests could also influence political debates in Europe, with governments facing pressure to address concerns over living standards and public services.You use AI every day. articles.title: UP's Pilibhit turtle carcass incinerated without autopsy, DFO asked to explain
articles.summary: PILIBHIT: Bareilly zone chief conservator of forests (CCF) P P Singh has sought an explanation from Pilibhit forest and wildlife division DFO Bharat Kumar
articles.body: PILIBHIT: Bareilly zone chief conservator of forests (CCF) P P Singh has sought an explanation from Pilibhit forest and wildlife division DFO Bharat Kumar DK after the carcass of an Indian flapshell turtle was incinerated without an autopsy or registration of a departmental case.The aquatic species is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. The CCF said the “handling of the carcass violated established protocols and standard operating procedures”.The crushed carcass was found on Pilibhit-Tanakpur Road, between a large water body and Drummond Government Inter College, around 10am Saturday. After being informed by local journalist Shubham Mishra, deputy range officer Sher Singh sent forest staff to collect it.However, divisional forest officials neither conducted an autopsy nor registered a departmental case. Both are mandatory under the protocol for dealing with the death of a Schedule I species.“A post-mortem examination must then be conducted by a panel of govt veterinary officers designated by a senior forest officer. For Schedule I species, videography of the procedure, site and carcass is mandatory. The examination involves documenting external and internal injuries and collecting biological samples, including visceral contents, tissue and blood, for forensic analysis,” the CCF said.Singh said forest staff must cordon off the site after a wildlife carcass is found to preserve evidence. They must photograph and videograph the undisturbed site, surrounding terrain and carcass, and look for signs of an accident, including vehicle-impact or collision marks.Singh said officials must also prepare site maps, record GPS coordinates, draw up seizure memos and make a general diary entry at the local police station. “A formal report must then be submitted to the state’s chief wildlife warden before the carcass is disposed of under official supervision.”He also directed the DFO to initiate a survey to identify aquatic wildlife species inhabiting the water body. He sought steps to stop the discharge of household wastewater and sewage into it, saying the pollution threatened protected aquatic wildlife.The CCF said pollution in the nearly one-hectare water body, a major portion of which is state-owned, would be raised with the district administration through the District Environment Committee. The panel is headed by the district magistrate, while the DFO serves as its secretary. Alleged encroachments on the water body would also be taken up by the committee, he added.Stay updated with the latest Bareilly news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Watch: French protesters loot Hermès, Apple and other luxury stores across cities
articles.summary: Looters ransacked luxury boutiques, electronics outlets, supermarkets and other businesses across several French cities on Saturday as protests against
articles.body: Looters ransacked luxury boutiques, electronics outlets, supermarkets and other businesses across several French cities on Saturday as protests against the rising cost of living descended into widespread violence, with authorities reporting mass arrests, injured police officers and fires.In Marseille, protesters vandalised dozens of shops, including luxury brand Hermès and stores selling jewellery, clothes, cosmetics, household appliances and bread, AFP reported. Firefighters also intervened to extinguish a blaze at a shoe shop.In Paris, looters smashed the window of a skincare store near République Square and threw beauty products to crowds gathered outside. A telecommunications shop was also broken into, with mobile phones tossed into the crowd. Nearby, a bar called La Barrique caught fire, while youths raided a supermarket and threw bottles and cans at police officers.Shops were also vandalised in Lille, where looters broke into an Apple Store in the city centre, according to Socialist mayor Arnaud Deslandes. In Nice, several businesses, including sportswear outlets and a motorcycle dealership, were targeted.The looting was part of wider unrest that erupted during nationwide demonstrations against inflation and declining purchasing power. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said late Saturday that 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers injured.Violence spreads across French citiesThe protests drew an estimated 550,000 participants nationwide, according to the interior ministry, while the CGT trade union put the figure at 800,000.Police used tear gas and water cannons against demonstrators who threw projectiles and fireworks. In the southern city of Saint-Etienne, a 17-year-old boy lost his right hand after being struck by a crowd-control grenade.Masked groups subsequently moved through several cities, setting fires, attacking businesses and breaking into shops to steal goods. AFP reporters in Paris observed groups of young men wearing masks and gloves disconnecting security cameras before smashing shop windows.Businesses targeted included supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing retailers, opticians, cosmetics stores and consumer electronics outlets in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg.Public buildings were also attacked. In Limoges, a fire largely destroyed the city's more than 140-year-old town hall after masked protesters broke into the building, according to the region's top official. Town halls in Marseille and Lille were also vandalised, while a police compound in Bordeaux was attacked and a tourist office in Lyon was set ablaze.President Emmanuel Macron vowed action against those responsible."those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting -- even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished," Macron said on X.Inflation fuels public anger ahead of electionsThe demonstrations reflect growing public anger over the cost of living, with purchasing power in France declining since 2024 and fuel prices rising following the US-Iran war earlier this year.The unrest also comes amid weeks of student protests and mounting criticism of the government over perceived police brutality against high-school students. France is preparing for presidential elections in 2027, with political uncertainty adding to the tensions.The demonstrations were supported by the Yellow Vest movement, which staged mass protests against Macron's government eight years ago over planned fuel tax increases. Saturday's mobilisation also drew protesters angry over inequality, political leadership and the concentration of wealth.In Paris, demonstrators chanted slogans against the police and called for Macron's resignation. Some protesters invoked the French Revolution, while others criticised politicians and the growing wealth of the ultra-rich.Opposition leaders sought to capitalise on the unrest. Far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen condemned the rioters and accused the party of her left-wing rival, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, of legitimising violence. Mélenchon, who had supported the demonstrations, urged protesters to avoid looting, calling it "contrary to our methods".The protests have intensified pressure on the French government as it confronts economic discontent, public anger over policing and a wave of violence across major urban centres.You use AI every day. articles.summary: CHENNAI: Heavy rain continued to lash Chennai overnight into Sunday, inundating several areas, with Ennore Port recording 222.5mm of rainfall in the 24
articles.body: CHENNAI: Heavy rain continued to lash Chennai overnight into Sunday, inundating several areas, with Ennore Port recording 222.5mm of rainfall in the 24 hours ending at 5.30am. The Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC) has forecast heavy to very heavy rain in Chennai and neighbouring areas on Sunday, while authorities have mobilised thousands of civic workers and disaster response teams to prepare for possible flooding.The RMC attributed the rainfall to a cyclonic circulation over northern Tamil Nadu and adjoining southern coastal Andhra Pradesh. Satellite imagery indicated significant convective cloud development over north coastal Tamil Nadu and adjoining sea areas.Across the city, Ennore, Tiruvottiyur and Manali were among the affected localities in North Chennai. Broadway, Prakasam Salai, Mannadi and Parry’s Corner also received very heavy rainfall, with some areas recording around 30cm.Additional chief secretary and commissioner B Chandra Mohan said Kathivakkam, Tiruvottiyur, Parry’s Corner, Sathanagadu, Meenambakkam and Basin Bridge had received around 30cm of rain. He warned that central and southern parts of Chennai could also experience heavy showers.Rainfall data for the 24 hours ending at 5.30am on Sunday showed that Nungambakkam recorded 157.8mm and Meenambakkam 146.7mm. Other locations that received heavy rain included YMCA Nandanam (148.5mm), Anna University (111mm) and Puzhal (77mm).Greater Chennai Corporation commissioner G S Sameeran said rainfall in some parts of the city had exceeded expectations. More than 15,000 sanitation and other civic workers had been deployed across Chennai through the night to manage the situation.The Tamil Nadu State Disaster Response Force had deployed 100 personnel as a precautionary measure. National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams were also being sent to the city to assist with emergency operations if flooding worsened.Automatic rain gauges across Chennai were transmitting readings every 15 minutes, allowing officials to monitor rainfall intensity. Public Works and Sports Development Minister Aadhav Arjuna was scheduled to inspect the situation at Ripon Buildings at 1.30am.Weather blogger Pradeep John described the rainfall as Chennai’s heaviest spell since Cyclone Michaung in December 2023, which brought around 400–450mm of rain in a day.“This is the heaviest rainfall Chennai has witnessed since Cyclone Michaung in December 2023, which brought around 400–450mm of rain in a day. After nearly 25 dry days, these rains arriving with the onset of the Northeast Monsoon make this spell even more special,” he said.Meanwhile, heavy rain is forecast in 17 Tamil Nadu districts on Sunday. Besides Chennai, Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram, the districts likely to receive heavy rain are Chengalpattu, the Nilgiris, Coimbatore, Dharmapuri, Krishnagiri, Salem, Villupuram, Kallakurichi, Cuddalore, Ariyalur, Tiruchirappalli, Perambalur, Tiruvannamalai and Erode.The RMC has also forecast heavy rain across several districts on Monday, including Chennai, Chengalpattu, Tiruvallur, Kancheepuram, Villupuram, Cuddalore, Mayiladuthurai, Nagapattinam, Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Pudukkottai, Ramanathapuram, Sivaganga, Thoothukudi, Kallakurichi, Ariyalur and Perambalur. Heavy rain accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning is also likely in Tiruchirappalli, the Nilgiris, Coimbatore and Tirunelveli.Chennai and its neighbouring districts feature in the forecasts for both days, while Monday’s outlook extends the possibility of heavy rain to parts of the Cauvery delta and southern Tamil Nadu.Separately, 4.15 lakh passengers travelled from Chennai to various parts of Tamil Nadu and other states on buses operated by state-owned transport corporations during the three days leading up to Ayudha Puja, according to the transport department.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.summary: Canadian billionaire and Shark Tank Judge Kevin O’Leary has said he no longer believes engineering is the only educational path that guarantees career
articles.body: Canadian billionaire and Shark Tank Judge Kevin O’Leary has said he no longer believes engineering is the only educational path that guarantees career success, arguing that storytelling and digital content creation have emerged among the most lucrative skills in today's economy. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), O'Leary said his views on education and high-demand careers have shifted significantly over the past few years as businesses increasingly rely on creators and digital marketers to acquire customers and grow revenue."I used to say just a few years ago, the only education you should get is engineering, engineering, and engineering. I don't believe that anymore," O'Leary wrote. According to O'Leary, skills such as storytelling, photography and video editing are reshaping the way both large and small companies attract customers. He said creators are becoming essential business partners because they help brands lower customer acquisition costs and improve returns on advertising spending.Kevin’O Leary believes creators changing how businesses find customersO’Leary said storytelling, photography, video editing and content creation are reshaping the landscape for both large and small businesses by helping them acquire customers.“It’s not a $48,000 career anymore, it’s more like a $400,000 career because they’re doing the contracts with multiple companies,” he said. He added that creators are showing companies how to reduce their customer acquisition cost and increase their return on ad spend. “That’s the opportunity,” he said. He ended with a nod to the creative fields: “It’s amazing what’s happening to the arts.”What 'O Leary meansCustomer acquisition cost is how much a business spends to win one new customer. Return on ad spend measures the revenue earned for every dollar spent on advertising. O’Leary’s argument is that creators who can produce content that brings in customers cheaply are being paid by several companies at once, rather than working for a single employer on a fixed salary. The $48,000 and $400,000 figures are O’Leary’s own and were not accompanied by a source. articles.body: Yemen’s government forces are trying to push back Houthi rebels, but a string of battlefield setbacks is raising a critical question: can they sustain the offensive before their own weaknesses derail it?According to an analysis published by Al Jazeera, the government is grappling with disrupted supply routes, the loss of strategic territory and difficulties coordinating rival military factions.Houthi advances have cut the main road linking Taiz to Aden and disrupted alternative mountain routes, leaving Taiz effectively besieged. The loss of the strategic Red Sea port of Mocha has further complicated the government's military position, while rising fuel prices in Taiz underscore the growing logistical strain on government-held areas.Colonel Wadah al-Dubaish, spokesperson for the government-aligned Joint Forces on Yemen’s West Coast, told Al Jazeera that Houthi attempts to cut supply routes had failed to stop the flow of essential supplies.“The Houthi group consistently attempts to sever supply lines to government forces, but they have been unable to halt these supplies. So, military operations against the Houthis will continue,” al-Dubaish told Al Jazeera.Al Jazeera reported that the challenges extend beyond supply disruptions and territorial losses, with the government also relying heavily on Saudi military support to sustain its campaign.Saudi air strikes have helped target Houthi positions and disrupt reinforcements, but air power alone cannot secure supply routes or guarantee that territory captured by government forces will remain under their control.Yemen’s government forces are also struggling to overcome divisions within their own ranks, with rival factions operating under different command structures complicating efforts to mount a coordinated offensive. These divisions contributed to the failure of anti-Houthi forces to respond quickly to the rebels’ advances along the Red Sea coast in September.Yemen’s deputy justice minister Faisal al-Majidi said that coordination between forces on the ground would be a decisive test for the campaign.“The coordination among various field forces … remains the true litmus test for the success of the Dawn of Yemen operation,” al-Majidi told Al Jazeera.The situation remains fluid, with Yemen’s government forces continuing operations on multiple fronts despite mounting logistical and military challenges.For Yemen’s government, the immediate challenge is to reopen supply routes, protect frontline positions and improve coordination among allied forces while maintaining Saudi support.The offensive has not been decisively defeated, but its ability to deliver lasting gains will depend on whether the government can overcome the logistical and command problems now threatening its campaign.You use AI every day.
